intro: Mahler’s Fifth ends in D major with a horn tune, chasing string parts and a brass chorale big enough to fill the hall. Even the preceding Adagietto gets up and dances.

sections.label: Intro · Horn, bassoon, oboe and clarinet
sections.mNote: Short wind phrases gather around a held horn A

sections.label: A · Horn tune and chasing strings
sections.mNote: A D-major tune leads into overlapping string entries

sections.label: Dev · The tunes change partners
sections.mNote: Wind melodies cross the strings’ continuing runs

cues.title: One A becomes a conversation
cues.text: The horn holds an A, the note left behind by the Adagietto. Bassoon, oboe and clarinet try out little phrases around it. The finale begins as a conversation among a few players, each putting a tune on the table.
cues.evidence: Peters full score, plate 9015, p. 183. Lew Smoley describes the linking A and introductory wind motifs: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/listening-guide/listening-guide-movement-5-rondo-finale-allegro-allegro-giocoso-frisch/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The horn finds a tune
cues.text: The horn gathers those small phrases into the rondo’s D-major tune. A second horn follows close behind. The melody has the sturdy gait of a country dance, with little falling figures that will keep turning up throughout the movement.
cues.evidence: Peters score, p. 183, Allegro commodo; Smoley describes the first horn’s theme, second-horn imitation and D-major setting.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cellos start the chase
cues.text: The cellos begin a running line before the previous phrase has quite finished. Other strings enter behind them and keep going. This is a fugato: one player’s arrival adds a new voice to the conversation without silencing the others.
cues.evidence: Peters score, pp. 185–186; Smoley identifies the cello upbeat overlapping the preceding cadence and the subsequent imitative entries.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The Adagietto learns to dance
cues.text: The finale borrows a melody from the Adagietto and sets it among quick string figures. Its long, yearning phrases acquire a spring in their step. Mahler’s direction for the transformed tune is schwungvoll — with swing.
cues.evidence: Smoley’s finale guide identifies the quotation of the Adagietto’s second theme, its quicker accompaniment and the marking Schwungvoll. This note concerns the recurring melody across the finale.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Bach beside the lake
cues.text: While writing the Fifth, Mahler is also living with Bach’s collected works, to which he subscribes. The finale sends its string parts after one another in fugues and canons, then lets a horn stroll through with a tune.
cues.evidence: Mahler Foundation, Symphony No. 5 introduction, on the Bach edition and the finale’s contrapuntal writing. https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-introduction/

cues.title: The bass gets the dance
cues.text: The big climb subsides and the dance tune drops into the bass. Scraps pass between low strings and woodwinds before the horns and violins take them up again. Mahler starts another ascent from this quieter floor.
cues.evidence: Smoley’s guide describes the late collapse into a bass statement of the main theme, followed by overlapping low-string and woodwind phrases and another ascent.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The chorale comes home
cues.text: The brass chorale from the second movement returns in D major. Quick strings run beneath its broad chords. Earlier, the hymn dissolved back into the storm; here it carries straight on towards the symphony’s finish.
cues.evidence: Peters score, p. 244, Pesante; Smoley identifies the chorale’s relation to movement II and its continuation into the coda.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A sharp last stroke
cues.text: The closing pages hurry into Presto. Horn calls and rushing strings seem ready to start another round, but Mahler cuts them short with the little figure from the introduction. A sharp stroke ends the symphony.
cues.evidence: Peters score, pp. 248–251, including Presto and the final short attacks; Smoley identifies the closing return of the introductory clarinet figure.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The oboe hands over to the horn
transitions.from: Intro · Horn, bassoon, oboe and clarinet
transitions.to: A · Horn tune and chasing strings
transitions.how: The oboe lingers on B♮. The horn takes that note into the main tune at Allegro commodo, with a second horn following in imitation. Open fifths in the accompaniment establish D major beneath the tune’s falling phrases.
transitions.evidence: Peters score, p. 183; Smoley describes the B♮ handover from oboe to horn and the D-major accompaniment.

transitions.title: The brass open into D major
transitions.from: Link · The tune sinks to the bass
transitions.to: Coda · Brass chorale and final rush
transitions.how: A long descending trombone line and horn calls usher in the D-major chorale. Mahler writes Pesante above its broad brass chords. The strings keep their quick figures moving underneath, carrying the hymn into the faster coda.
transitions.evidence: Peters score, pp. 244–248; Smoley describes the trombone descent, horn calls and return of the second movement’s chorale.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 5, V, Peters study score, plate 9015
source.locator: Printed p. 183: horn and woodwind introduction; pp. 185–186: string fugato; p. 210: horn and string melody; pp. 244–251: brass chorale and closing pages.

timeline.note: A horn note sets off short replies from bassoon, oboe and clarinet.
The horn carries the rondo tune above woodwinds and low strings.
Cellos start the fugato; other string sections take up the running line.
Horn and strings sing longer phrases above held woodwind notes.
The brass chorale rises above running strings and the full orchestra.
Fast orchestral figures rush towards the short closing chords.
The written finale closes in D major.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
